source.title: Extreme Learning Machine Design for Dealing with Unrepresentative Features
source.authors: Nicolás Nieto; F. Ibarrola; V. Peterson; H. Rufiner; Rubén D. Spies

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps hidden-layer size in an Extreme Learning Machine (ELM), a different model and setting from the deep-network claim, and reports test performance as size changes.
record.gate_note: The paper cites a similar multilayer-perceptron result from another study; that cited result is not recorded as this study's evidence. Figure 5 compares pruning and growing methods, but its method-comparison results do not separately establish the unpruned ELM size curve. The disconnected-neuron weight measurement is recorded as a related finding, not as a test-error result.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps hidden-layer size in Extreme Learning Machines, which are random-feature single-hidden-layer networks rather than deep networks. It reports test accuracy falling to a minimum at M=N and rising again for M>N on EEG data. This is a result on the general double-descent curve (V4) in a new model class and setting. It does not test deep networks (V1), epochs, samples, effective complexity, label noise or regularization.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also argue that choosing M close to N causes overfitting while M>>N can perform significantly better, depending on the data. They explain this by the model's ability to neglect irrelevant features once M>N.
record.recipe_differences: Uses randomly initialized ELM hidden layers and least-squares output weights, tested on synthetic and EEG classification data; it does not reproduce the original deep-network setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported benefit of larger hidden layers depends on data characteristics: the authors state that clean two-coordinate synthetic data favors small M, while more unrepresentative features make larger M more advantageous.

fits_no_version.finding: The output weight on an added class-uncorrelated neuron stays small until M approaches N, then decays for M>N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Past the interpolation threshold, minimum-norm ELM solutions down-weight irrelevant features, explaining the second descent.

fits_no_version.finding: The advantage of M>>N over small M grows with the number of uninformative input features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of the overparameterized regime in random-feature networks depends on input-feature noise.

record.problems: The direct size-sweep curve is reported for one EEG dataset; the synthetic curves provide no numerical values in the text. The paper's table comparisons use selected methods and do not independently show a full curve around the interpolation point.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 results for RBP, FWD, and random pruning are method-comparison curves rather than a separate unpruned size-sweep result; they are noted in gate_note but not extracted as claim rows.

untested.parts: Only ELMs are tested, not multiple model classes. Risk is not shown to diverge at the threshold. Subsumption of the classical U-curve is not tested.
Deep networks are not tested; ELMs have one random hidden layer.
No label-noise or regularization sweep; no multiple descent.

missing.what: FWD curves are standard unpruned ELMs retrained at each M (Algorithm 2), so they are a size sweep. The text says performance is '(somewhat) monotonically increasing for M > N' on one DaSalla subject and one P300 subject. rows_left_out wrongly treats them as method comparison only.
Per-subject P300 AUC and size for STD/FWD/RBP (subjects S1–S5); figure only.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Belkin et al. (an original source) for the matching MLP behaviour; that cited result is not this study's evidence. N is not reported for any experiment, so the M=N location rests on the authors' statement. No numeric curve values are given; the second-descent evidence is text plus figures. RBP rows were unlinked as the study's own method.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests ELMs, not deep networks.
No epoch- or training-time sweep is reported.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold is reported.
Only ELMs are tested; the study does not test double descent across multiple model classes or establish that it subsumes the classical U-shaped curve.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
No label-noise or regularization sweep, or test for triple or multiple descent, is reported.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters.

rows.subject: ELM
rows.size_stated: STD: M< N; FWD: up to M*=1000
rows.operation_detail: Compared the traditional M<N setting (STD) with the forward growing scheme (FWD).
rows.note: The larger-size method has higher reported accuracy than STD, but this table does not itself show a complete curve around the interpolation point. FWD size is reported as 28.2 ± 10.6 × 10^3.
rows.check: Selection values: STD is the best M<N and FWD is a validation-selected growing scheme. The size is misattributed: on DaSalla (Table 1) FWD M=228±76 and STD M=24±18. The 28.2±10.6×10^3 figure belongs to Table 2 (P300).

rows.subject: ELM

rows.note: The larger-size method has higher reported accuracy than STD, but this table does not itself show a complete curve around the interpolation point.
rows.check: RBP is the study's own pruning method compared with others; it should not be a claim row. The size is also misattributed: DaSalla RBP M=209±151, not 14.5×10^3.

relationships.condition: ELM size sweep on DaSalla EEG, and synthetic data with junk features (TF=8, 32)
relationships.reason: Test accuracy hits its global minimum at M=N and rises again for M>N; with junk features M>>N is preferable (r4, r2, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy reached its global minimum at M=N and rose for M>N, with M≫N preferable when junk features were present.

relationships.condition: Validation-selected larger ELMs vs best M<N on DaSalla and P300
relationships.reason: FWD beats STD: 0.669 vs 0.622 accuracy (r6), 0.816 vs 0.718 AUC (r8). These are selection comparisons, not curves.
relationships.display_finding: Validation-selected larger ELMs achieved 0.669 versus 0.622 accuracy and 0.816 versus 0.718 AUC for the smaller-model comparison.

relationships.condition: Clean synthetic data without junk features (TF=0)
relationships.reason: Authors state small M is optimal here, so the overparameterized regime gives no advantage over the classical optimum (r1).
relationships.display_finding: A small M was optimal, and overparameterization provided no advantage over the classical optimum.
